name: Waspie

card.summary: A short, boned waist cincher worn over the midsection to give an instantly smaller waist and a more pronounced hourglass line.
card.note: Extreme tight lacing is reported historically to cause rib deformity and organ displacement.

quick.overview:
A waspie is a short, back-laced corset or belt, usually about six to seven inches long, worn snugly at the waist. It compresses the midsection so the waist looks smaller and the hips and bust look relatively fuller.
The look is temporary and lasts while the garment is worn. It became the signature undergarment of Christian Dior's 1947 New Look, which featured a wasp-waisted silhouette.
quick.how: A waspie is worn over a girdle or against the body under clothes, laced or closed at the back or front. Elastic-backed styles are also worn visibly as a belt to accent an outfit. Boned styles give back support.
quick.risks: Historical writing on extreme tight lacing reports deformed ribs, weakened abdominal muscles, displaced organs and breathing problems. Ordinary light waspies are not described as having those effects.

lead: A waist cincher, also called a waspie or guepiere, is a belt worn around the waist to make it look or feel smaller.[1] Short corsets date to at least 1860, and Christian Dior's New Look popularised the cincher around 1947, with the waspie as its signature undergarment.[1]

Waspies were typically boned and back-laced, usually six to seven inches long, and worn snugly over a girdle.[1] They create the wasp-waist silhouette: a sharp transition from the rib cage to a small waist with hips curving out below.[2] Elastic-backed belts with front closures are worn to define the waist or accent an outfit.[1]

chain: Short boned band is laced snugly over the waist
Smaller waist and more pronounced hourglass line while worn
angle.text: A waspie is worn to give an immediate, temporary hourglass shape. Clothes drape over the narrower waist, making hips and bust read as fuller.

infobox: Boned, back-laced, worn over a girdle[1]

paras: Short one-part corsets existed by 1860, and ribbon corsets of silk and bones were home-sewn around 1901.[1] After the Second World War, the New Look brought back the wasp-waist silhouette and the waspie became its signature undergarment; designer Anne Fogarty promoted the look in the US.[1][2]

Short corsets were worn for light support, against the skin or over clothing.[1] Boned underbust styles give more back support and are sometimes presented as a fashionable alternative to certain medical back braces.[1]

Tight lacing, using increasingly tight corsets over time, began in the late 1820s and 1830s after steel eyelets made tighter lacing possible.[3] Wikipedia's wasp-waist article reports that extreme tight lacing could deform ribs, weaken abdominal muscles, displace organs and cause respiratory ailments.[2] Doctors and dress reformers of the era strongly opposed the practice.[3]

timeline.event: Short corsets of one part exist by at least this date.[1]
